section.title: Authority and the Parable of the Tenants
section.sectionRationale: The leaders challenge Jesus' authority, and He answers with a counter-question and two vineyard parables. The two sons expose a religion of words without obedience; the wicked tenants indict leaders who reject God's messengers and will kill His Son, and announce that the kingdom will be given to a fruit-bearing people.
section.thesis: Jesus' authority is from heaven, and the leaders who reject it prove, like the disobedient son and the murderous tenants, to be fruitless and self-condemned; the rejected Son is God's cornerstone, and the kingdom is given to a people who bear its fruit.
section.frameNote: Three beats: the challenge to Jesus' authority and the question about John; the parable of the two sons; and the parable of the wicked tenants with the rejected cornerstone.

verses.text: When Jesus returned to the temple courts and began to teach, the chief priests and elders of the people came up to Him. “By what {{exousia|authority}} are You doing these things?” they asked. “And who gave You this authority?”
“I will also ask you one question,” Jesus replied, “and if you answer Me, I will tell you by what authority I am doing these things.
What was the source of John’s baptism? Was it from heaven or from men?” They deliberated among themselves and said, “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ He will ask, ‘Why then did you not believe him?’
But if we say, ‘From men,’ we are afraid of the people, for they all regard John as a prophet.”
So they answered, “We do not know.” And Jesus replied, “Neither will I tell you by what authority I am doing these things.

units.label: The parable of the two sons

verses.text: But what do you think? There was a man who had two sons. He went to the first one and said, ‘Son, go and work today in the vineyard.’
‘I will not,’ he replied. But later he changed his mind and went.
Then the man went to the second son and told him the same thing. ‘I will, sir,’ he said. But he did not go.
Which of the two did the will of his father?” “The first,” they answered. Jesus said to them, “Truly I tell you, the tax collectors and prostitutes are entering the kingdom of God before you.
For John came to you in the way of righteousness, and you did not believe him, but the tax collectors and prostitutes did. And even after you saw this, you did not repent and believe him.

Listen to another parable: There was a landowner who planted a vineyard. He put a wall around it, dug a winepress in it, and built a tower. Then he rented it out to some tenants and went away on a journey.
When the harvest time drew near, he sent his servants to the tenants to collect his share of the fruit.
But the tenants seized his servants. They beat one, killed another, and stoned a third.
Again, he sent other servants, more than the first group. But the tenants did the same to them.
Finally, he sent his son to them. ‘They will respect my son,’ he said.
But when the tenants saw the son, they said to one another, ‘This is the heir. Come, let us kill him and take his inheritance.’
So they seized him and threw him out of the vineyard and killed him.
Therefore, when the owner of the vineyard returns, what will he do to those tenants?”
“He will bring those wretches to a wretched end,” they replied, “and will rent out the vineyard to other tenants who will give him his share of the fruit at harvest time.”
Jesus said to them, “Have you never read in the Scriptures: ‘The {{lithos|stone}} the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. This is from the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes’?
Therefore I tell you that the kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a people who will produce its {{karpos|fruit}}.
He who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces, but he on whom it falls will be crushed.”
When the chief priests and Pharisees heard His parables, they knew that Jesus was speaking about them.
Although they wanted to arrest Him, they were afraid of the crowds, because the people regarded Him as a prophet.

exousia.gloss: Authority, the right and power to act. The leaders demand the source of Jesus' authority; He exposes that they will not honestly reckon with heaven's authority in John, and so forfeit the right to His answer. His authority is from the Father.

lithos.gloss: A stone. Quoting Psalm 118, Jesus is the stone the builders rejected that becomes the cornerstone; the very Son the tenants kill is the foundation of God's new building, and the stone that saves also judges those who stumble on it.

karpos.gloss: Fruit, produce, the yield the owner rightly seeks. The vineyard was to give its fruit to God; because the tenants withhold it, the kingdom is given to a people who will produce its fruit, the mark of true belonging to God.

basic.context: Back in the temple, the chief priests and elders demand to know by what authority Jesus acts. He answers with a question about John's baptism they will not answer honestly, so He declines to answer them. Then He tells two parables. In the first, one son says no but obeys, another says yes but does not, and the leaders, like the second, are outdone by tax collectors and prostitutes who repented. In the second, tenants beat and kill the owner's servants and finally his son; the kingdom, Jesus says, will be taken from them and given to a fruit-bearing people, for the rejected stone is now the cornerstone.
basic.hermeneutics: These are confrontation parables aimed squarely at the leaders, who understand that Jesus means them. The vineyard is Israel, the servants are the prophets, the son is Jesus, and the tenants are the current leadership. The point is not merit but response: honest repentance and fruit versus a religion of words. The cornerstone quotation reframes Jesus' coming rejection as God's plan.
basic.originalLanguages: The leaders demand the source of Jesus' exousia, authority, but forfeit His answer. Jesus is the lithos, the stone, rejected by the builders yet made the cornerstone. And the kingdom goes to a people who produce its karpos, its fruit.
basic.typology: The vineyard fulfills Isaiah 5, God's vineyard Israel. The rejected stone become cornerstone is Psalm 118, fulfilled in Christ crucified and risen. The killed son foreshadows the cross itself.
basic.christ: Jesus is the beloved Son sent last of all, rejected and killed outside the vineyard, yet raised to become the cornerstone of God's new building. He is the authority the leaders will not own and the stone on which people are either built or broken.
basic.god: God is the patient owner who sends servant after servant and at last His own Son, and the just judge who will remove the kingdom from fruitless stewards and give it to those who bear fruit. He turns the rejected Son into the cornerstone.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 5 is the song of the vineyard behind the parable. Psalm 118 gives the rejected stone. Acts 4 applies the cornerstone to Christ before these same leaders. 1 Peter 2 develops the stone that saves and stumbles.
basic.oneStory: In the temple He came to claim, Jesus exposes the leaders who reject heaven's authority, and in two parables He unveils the whole story: God's vineyard, His prophets rejected, His Son sent and killed, and the kingdom given to a fruit-bearing people. The rejected Son becomes the cornerstone. The plot of the passion is laid bare, and the leaders, understanding, only harden, unable to arrest Him yet because of the crowds.

context.literary:
The section is a duel of questions fought in the temple courts, and it is built in four panels that tighten like a net. First comes the leaders' challenge about authority, verses 23 to 27. Then Jesus answers with a counter-question, and the leaders' calculating reply, 'We do not know,' is the hinge of the whole passage. Two parables follow, and each ends by making the hearers condemn themselves: 'The first,' verse 31, and 'He will bring those wretches to a wretched end,' verse 41. Matthew then gives a quotation from Scripture, a verdict on the kingdom, and an observation about what the leaders understood, verses 42 to 46.

The two parables are paired deliberately and are bracketed by vineyards. The first is about a father who sends sons to work in his vineyard, the second about an owner who sends servants and then a son to collect fruit from it. The first is about response, and the second is about history. Together they answer the opening question: Jesus' authority comes from the Father, as John's did, and the proper reply to a sent one is obedience. The leaders asked for His credentials; the parables show them what they are doing with them.

Matthew uses a trapped-in-their-own-words device throughout. In the first exchange the leaders reason aloud, 'If we say... but if we say...' in verses 25 and 26, so that Matthew lets the reader hear them think. In the second and third scenes Jesus asks, 'What do you think?' verse 28, and 'what will he do to those tenants?' verse 40, and the leaders pronounce their own sentence. By verse 45 they understand it, and the narrator says so, which is why the passage ends in fear rather than debate. The leaders are afraid of the crowds in verse 26 and in verse 46. The two fears frame the whole section and reveal what governs them: not conscience but popularity.

The section also has a quiet architecture of 'give' and 'receive.' The authority is said to be 'given' in verse 23, the vineyard is rented out, the kingdom will be 'taken away' and 'given' in verse 43. Everything in the story is a trust, and the question throughout is what is done with a trust.
context.historical:
The chief priests and elders were the two ruling bodies of the Sanhedrin that met in Jerusalem, and they had the most to lose when a Galilean teacher began acting in their temple. Their question, 'Who gave You this authority?', was a legal one. A teacher without a recognized line of ordination, no priestly family and no rabbinic school, was asking for trouble. Jesus has just overturned the tables and healed in the courts, so the question presses the claim He has made by action.

John's baptism was the unavoidable test. John had drawn crowds from Jerusalem and all Judea, Matthew 3:5, and the people regarded him as a prophet, verse 26. The leaders had not committed to him, which is why their dilemma is so sharp. To say 'from heaven' was to admit they should have believed. To say 'from men' was to risk the crowd, who held John as a prophet, and in Jerusalem during Passover week a riot was a real danger. Such crowds were the reason the Roman governor was in the city.

The vineyard image would have been instantly recognized. Israel as God's vine was an ancient commonplace, Psalm 80:8-16, Isaiah 5:1-7, Jeremiah 2:21, Hosea 10:1. The details of the owner's work, a wall, a winepress and a tower, are Isaiah's own, and some ancient Jewish readers of Isaiah 5 took the tower and winepress to be the sanctuary and altar, which would make the parable a story about the temple leadership itself. The business arrangement is also credible. Absentee landlords in the hill country of Galilee and Judea leased land to tenants who paid a share of produce, and disputes over rent sometimes turned violent. Jesus' hearers did not need to be told that such a story was realistic.

The tenants' reasoning in verse 38, that killing the heir would leave the vineyard theirs, is often explained by the thought that, with no heir left to claim it, the tenants in possession might hope to keep the land. Whether or not the law would have worked that way, it is the logic of greed. The story is plausible as a story and, as a picture of the nation's history, only too accurate: the prophets had been mocked, imprisoned and killed, Nehemiah 9:26, 2 Chronicles 36:15-16, and Jesus will say as much in Matthew 23:29-37.
context.canonical:
The parable of the tenants rests on Isaiah's Song of the Vineyard, Isaiah 5:1-7. There the owner does everything for his vineyard, expects good grapes, and gets sour ones. Isaiah's interpretation is that the vineyard is the house of Israel and the LORD looked for justice but saw bloodshed. Jesus keeps the setting and changes the failing: in Isaiah the fault is in the vines, and in Jesus' version it is in the tenants, the leaders to whom the vineyard was entrusted. Jeremiah had said the same of the shepherds, Jeremiah 23:1-2, and Ezekiel 34 had said it again.

The cornerstone saying is Psalm 118:22-23, the same psalm the crowd sang in Matthew 21:9. The leaders, who had a few days earlier heard 'Hosanna' from the pilgrims, are now told that the stone of that psalm is the one they are rejecting. Isaiah 28:16 and Isaiah 8:14 also speak of a stone in Zion, one a sure foundation and the other a stone of stumbling, and the early church combined them. Peter applies the cornerstone to Jesus before the same council, Acts 4:11, and in 1 Peter 2:4-8 he links all three texts. Paul does the same in Romans 9:32-33, and Ephesians 2:20-22 builds the church on that stone.

The saying about the stone that crushes, verse 44, draws on Daniel 2:34-35 and 44-45, where a stone cut without human hands breaks the empires and becomes a mountain that fills the earth. The kingdom that Daniel saw growing from a stone is the kingdom now being taken from unfaithful stewards and given to others. John the Baptist had already warned that the axe was at the root and that God could raise up children for Abraham from stones, Matthew 3:9-10, so the theme of stones and fruit is Matthew's own thread.

The parable of the two sons speaks into Ezekiel 18:21-28, where a wicked man who turns lives and a righteous man who turns away dies, and echoes the plain teaching of Matthew 7:21 that not everyone who says 'Lord, Lord' enters the kingdom, but the one who does the Father's will.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Matthew places this section at the head of a long run of controversies in order to show that the rejection of Jesus was neither hasty nor hidden. He had been given every sign, heard from John, and been warned in parable, and the leaders knew what the parables meant. For Matthew's first readers, a mix of Jewish and Gentile believers who could ask why the people who had the Scriptures did not receive their Messiah, the answer is given by the owner of the vineyard: a patient God sent messenger after messenger, and the last messenger was His own Son.

Matthew also wanted his church to examine itself. The first parable is aimed at religious people who say yes and do nothing, and it is a standing warning to any community that has the language of obedience. The second ends with a kingdom entrusted to 'a people who will produce its fruit,' and that clause is addressed to the church as much as it is spoken against the leaders. The Gospel will end with the Great Commission, and the fruit that God seeks is the discipleship that is described there.

Finally, the evangelist wants his readers to see that Jesus goes to the cross knowingly. The parable shows Him describing His own death, and its place in the plan of God, days before it happens. Nothing in the passion takes Him by surprise.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The words about the leaders describe a particular generation of stewards at a particular crisis. It would be a serious misuse to read them as a charge against the Jewish people, or against any people. The parable is told by a Jewish teacher, to Jewish leaders, in the Jewish temple, about a vineyard that belongs to the God of Israel, and the first disciples and most of the first church were Jews. The transfer of the kingdom in verse 43 is a change of tenants, not the cancelling of the vineyard.

What is prescribed is the response of the first son: say no and then repent and go. Matthew's word for his change of heart in verse 29 is the word used of the leaders' failure in verse 32, so the Gospel's call is that whoever has said no can still turn and work. The passage also prescribes honest answers. The leaders' 'We do not know' in verse 27 is a lie of convenience, and Jesus refuses to reward it. Followers of Jesus are called to truthfulness before the truth even when it is costly, and to take care that their religious position does not make them deaf. Whoever holds an office in the church holds it as a tenant, accountable for fruit that belongs to the Owner.

debates.question: Does the kingdom pass from Israel to the church?

views.label: Replacement: the church takes Israel's place
views.case: Verse 43 says the kingdom will be taken away from 'you' and given to 'a people,' and the same Gospel ends by sending the disciples to all nations. Some see here a straightforward transfer from the old covenant people to the new, supported by Acts 13:46 where Paul turns to the Gentiles and by 1 Peter 2:9, where the church is called a chosen people and a holy nation.

views.label: Transfer of stewardship: new leaders and a renewed people
views.case: The parable's tenants are the leaders, not the nation, and the new tenants are those who will give fruit. The first disciples were Jewish, and the church began as a Jewish movement in the same city. Paul says that God has not rejected His people, Romans 11:1, and that branches broken off can be grafted in again, Romans 11:23-24. On this view the vineyard remains Israel's, enlarged by grafted branches.

views.label: A warning with the door still open
views.case: The whole passage invites repentance. The first parable's open door for those who changed their minds, and the stone that crushes only if it falls on someone, suggest that the judgment is conditional. Peter, a few weeks later, preaches to the same city and thousands respond, Acts 2:41.

debates.bearing: The text itself speaks of a people, a leadership and a fruit, and not of ethnic replacement. The safest reading holds that the stewards are removed, that the vineyard is opened to all nations, and that Paul's metaphor of the olive tree guards against any boast on the part of the Gentile believer.

debates.question: Is the stone a cornerstone or a capstone?

views.label: The cornerstone at the foundation
views.case: The word used in the Greek Old Testament, literally 'head of the corner,' is most naturally understood as the stone laid at the corner of the foundation, from which the building is squared. Isaiah 28:16 speaks of a precious cornerstone and a sure foundation, and Ephesians 2:20 uses the foundation image for Christ.

views.label: The capstone at the top
views.case: Others take the phrase to mean the final stone set at the summit or the keystone of an arch, the last piece that completes the structure. Zechariah 4:7 speaks of bringing forth the capstone to shouts of 'Grace, grace,' and the image of a stone rejected and then crowned fits the resurrection as the moment of vindication.

debates.bearing: Either picture serves Matthew's purpose. The rejected stone becomes the stone on which everything else depends, whether at the bottom or at the top, and the saying about falling on it and being crushed by it works with both.

study.originalLanguages:
The word exousia in verse 23 is built on a verb meaning 'it is permitted,' and its first sense is the right to act, authority granted, not simply power. The question has two halves: by what authority, and who gave it. The leaders think in terms of credentials. Matthew uses the word for Jesus again and again: the crowds saw that He taught 'as one who had authority,' Matthew 7:29, He claims authority on earth to forgive sins, Matthew 9:6, and He closes the Gospel with 'All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me,' Matthew 28:18. The leaders' question is answered, in the end, by the whole book. The 'given' in that last verse matches the 'who gave You' of verse 23.

Jesus' counter-question speaks of John's baptism as being 'from heaven or from men.' In Matthew's idiom 'heaven' is a reverent way of speaking of God, and the dilemma is whether John's mission came from God or from human invention. When the leaders reason aloud, the Greek has them literally 'reasoning among themselves,' and the content of their reasoning is entirely about consequences. The word for their final answer, 'We do not know,' is the plain verb for knowing, and it is a conscious refusal.

In the first parable the key verb is in verse 29: the first son 'changed his mind' and went. The Greek is metamelomai, a word of regret or change of heart, and it returns in verse 32 where the leaders 'did not repent and believe him.' It is also the verb used of Judas when he sees that Jesus is condemned, Matthew 27:3. Its meaning is a change of mind accompanied by feeling, and what separates the first son from Judas is where regret leads: the son goes and works, and Judas goes and hangs himself. Regret alone is not enough; it must turn into obedience. The manuscripts also vary in the order of the sons and in which one is said to be obedient, but the point holds in every form of the text, that the one who does the will of the father is the one who goes.

In verse 31, Jesus says the tax collectors and prostitutes are 'entering' the kingdom before the leaders. The verb is proago, to go ahead or to lead the way, and it is a present tense. It does not say that the leaders are shut out forever; it says that others are going in front. The door is open and a procession is already moving through it.

The tenants are georgoi, farmers or workers of the land, and the owner 'rented out' the vineyard, a verb for leasing. The tenants say of the son, 'This is the heir,' verse 38, and use the word kleronomos. The phrase 'Come, let us kill him' is almost identical to what the brothers say about Joseph in Genesis 37:20, 'Come now, let us kill him.' Matthew's readers who knew Genesis would hear the old story of the beloved son sold by his own family and exalted, and would sense that this one too will be exalted.

The Hebrew of Psalm 118:22 has a wordplay that Greek loses: ben is 'son' and eben is 'stone.' The parable moves from the son who is killed in verse 39 to the stone that is raised in verse 42, and the connection is more than coincidence. The rejected 'son' is the rejected 'stone.' The verb of the quotation, 'rejected,' is apodokimazo, to test and then disqualify, as a builder rejects a stone after inspecting it. The builders have had the stone in their hands and decided it was not fit.

Verse 43 says the kingdom will be given to an ethnos, the Greek word for a nation or people, in the singular, 'a people who will produce its fruit.' The fruit is plural in the Greek, 'its fruits,' which is the way Matthew speaks of the visible results of a life, as in Matthew 7:16-20 and 12:33. And the words in verse 44 about falling on the stone and the stone falling on someone are missing from a few early manuscripts and are similar to Luke 20:18, so some editors treat the verse with caution, though it is read in the great majority of manuscripts and fits Matthew's context well.

typology.type: The vineyard and its keepers, Isaiah 5 and Psalm 80
typology.fulfillment: Israel is the vine brought out of Egypt and planted, Psalm 80:8-16, and the LORD's vineyard in Isaiah's song, Isaiah 5:1-7. Jesus takes the old symbol and adds the tenants and the sent Son. The escalation is that in Isaiah the vineyard is trampled and left a wasteland, but here the vineyard itself is not destroyed; it is rented to others. John 15:1 then carries the image forward when Jesus says 'I am the true vine,' so that the fruit God seeks from Israel is found in the one Israelite who bears it perfectly and in those who abide in Him. The type falls short in that earlier vines could fail; this Vine cannot.

typology.type: The sent servants and the prophets, Jeremiah 7:25
typology.fulfillment: The long line of servants in verses 34 to 36 matches the history in Jeremiah 7:25-26, where God says He sent His servants the prophets again and again. 2 Chronicles 36:15-16 gives the pattern: messengers sent from compassion, mocked and despised until there was no remedy. Hebrews 1:1-2 draws the contrast that the parable dramatizes, that God spoke through the prophets but in these last days through a Son whom He appointed heir of all things. The sequence is an escalation from servants to Son, and the type is exceeded in that the Son is not another messenger but the heir Himself.

typology.type: The beloved son rejected, Joseph and the cross
typology.fulfillment: The tenants' words, 'Come, let us kill him,' echo the brothers' plot against Joseph, Genesis 37:20. Joseph, the favored son sent by his father to his brothers, is stripped and thrown into a pit, and then raised to rule, so that the story of rejection ends in rescue for those who rejected him, Genesis 50:20. In the parable the son is thrown out of the vineyard, and Hebrews 13:12 says Jesus suffered outside the city gate. The correspondence is that the one the father sends is the one the keepers reject, and the escalation is that Jesus' rejection is not merely survived but becomes the foundation of a new building. Joseph's exaltation was in Egypt; Christ's is at the right hand of the Father.

typology.type: The stone that the builders rejected, Psalm 118:22
typology.fulfillment: The psalm celebrates a king or a people who were despised and then vindicated by God, and the early church read it as fulfilled in the resurrection, Acts 4:10-11. The stone of Daniel 2, cut without hands, which breaks the empires and becomes a mountain, Daniel 2:34-35, supplies the second half: the stone that rises also falls on its enemies, verse 44. Paul says the church is built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets with Christ Jesus Himself as the cornerstone, Ephesians 2:20. The type is exceeded in that the stone is not an object but a living person, 1 Peter 2:4, and those who rest on Him are themselves made into a temple.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ in a way that is rare in the Gospels: Jesus tells His own story in advance. The son sent last of all, after the servants, whom the tenants seize, throw out and kill, is a portrait of the cross. Mark and Luke call him a beloved son, and Matthew has already twice heard the voice from heaven, 'This is My beloved Son,' Matthew 3:17 and 17:5. The parable is therefore a bridge between the voice at the Jordan and the voice at the cross. What the leaders will do in a few days is exactly what the parable says, and they do it with eyes open, since the narrator states that they understood the parable was about them.

Jesus is also the one who answers the question of authority. The leaders ask who gave it, and His reply shows that He stands in the line of John and the prophets but at the end of it. The Gospel will give the full answer at the end: 'All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me,' Matthew 28:18, a verse that echoes the language of Daniel 7:13-14, where one like a son of man is given dominion, glory and a kingdom that will never be destroyed. The authority of Jesus is not a delegated permission to teach but the authority of the Son who inherits.

The stone is the place where the parable moves from tragedy to triumph. The one rejected is raised: 'This is from the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes.' The resurrection is the Lord's reversal of the builders' verdict. Peter says so to the same council in Acts 4:10-12, and adds that there is salvation in no one else. The stone is not a neutral foundation; it divides. Those who fall on it in repentance are broken and are remade, while those on whom it falls are crushed. Simeon had said that this child was set for the falling and rising of many in Israel, Luke 2:34, and the picture here is the grown-up version.

The parable also shows what kind of king Jesus is, since the owner of the vineyard is patient. The Son comes unarmed and unprotected, trusting the tenants to respect Him. His gentleness at the entry is repeated in this story as vulnerability. He is also the Son who is the inheritance: the tenants kill Him to take what is His, but the Father gives the vineyard to the Son's people and raises the Son as head of the building.

We should not make a code of every detail. The tower, the winepress and the wall serve the story and do not each need a meaning. The links to Christ that carry weight are the ones that the Gospel itself draws: the son who is killed, the stone that is raised, and the authority given by the Father.
study.god:
The owner of the vineyard is the portrait of God's patience. He plants and equips, he trusts the vineyard to others and goes away, and when the fruit is not delivered he does not at once destroy but sends servants, and then more servants, and then his son. This is the pattern of Scripture, as Jeremiah 7:25 put it: 'again and again.' The long suffering of God is not weakness but a persistence in giving people every chance. The line in verse 37, 'They will respect my son,' is not naive; it expresses the hope of a father who has already given everything.

God is also the one who has rights. The vineyard is His, the fruit is His share, and the tenants are accountable. The parable is blunt about the fact that everything entrusted to human hands is a lease, not a possession. God's claim on what is His is the ground of His judgment, and that judgment is not arbitrary: the tenants have beaten, killed and stoned. The leaders themselves pronounce the sentence in verse 41, and Jesus does not add to it. A holy God who does not judge such a record would not be good.

But the passage ends with God's own action in reverse. The builders reject, and the Lord reverses the verdict, and the psalm says, 'This is from the LORD.' The tenants' plot to seize the inheritance is part of a story God has been writing. It does not make the killing right, since the leaders are guilty, but it shows that human wickedness cannot undo the plan of God. The cross is both the worst of human crimes and the fulfilment of God's purpose, a tension that Peter holds together in Acts 2:23 when he says that Jesus was handed over by God's deliberate plan and nailed to a cross by the hands of the lawless.

God is the giver of the kingdom. It is taken from some and 'given' to others, and the word suggests grace. The people who receive it do not earn it by being better, as the first parable shows with the surprise that tax collectors and prostitutes enter first. But the gift carries an expectation of fruit, and this holds justice and mercy together: the God who gives freely also expects the harvest.

For worship, this means thankfulness and fear together. Thankfulness, because the vineyard is a gift and the rejected Son has become our cornerstone, marvelous in our eyes. Fear, because stewardship is real and the God who sends servants and a Son is not mocked. The right response is the first son's: to turn, go and work.

crossReferences.note: The song of the vineyard supplies the setting and the details of the parable: the hill, the cleared stones, the tower, the winepress, and the owner who looked for good grapes. Isaiah's verdict is that the LORD looked for justice and saw bloodshed. Jesus narrows the charge from the whole vineyard to its keepers.

The vine brought from Egypt and planted by God, then ravaged because its walls were broken down. The psalm pleads for the vine and for 'the son You have raised up for Yourself.' The parable of the tenants gives the answer to that prayer: God sends His Son to the vineyard.

The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone, and the psalmist says this is the LORD's doing. Jesus quotes it directly after the parable, and the same psalm was on the crowd's lips a few verses earlier at the entry, so the leaders hear the Hosanna and the warning from the same song.

The brothers see Joseph coming and say, 'Come now, let us kill him.' The words of the tenants about the heir in Matthew 21:38 are nearly the same. The echo turns the parable into the old story of the beloved son rejected by his own family, and it carries the hint that rejection will end in exaltation.

The chronicler summarizes Israel's history as God sending messengers again and again out of compassion, and the people mocking them until there was no remedy. It is the story the parable compresses into three verses, the beaten, killed and stoned servants of verse 35.

A stone cut without human hands strikes the statue and becomes a mountain that fills the earth. Matthew 21:44 speaks of a stone that falls and crushes. The kingdom Daniel saw is the kingdom that Jesus says is being taken from the tenants and given to a people who bear fruit.

Peter stands before the rulers, elders and scribes, and says that Jesus Christ, whom they crucified, is the stone you builders rejected, and that salvation is in no one else. It is the parable put into preaching, addressed to the same council.

Peter combines three stone texts, Isaiah 28:16, Psalm 118:22 and Isaiah 8:14, and sets them out as two responses: precious to those who believe, a stone of stumbling to those who do not. He also says believers are being built into a spiritual house, which is the positive side of the parable.

Paul explains Israel's stumbling in the same terms: the people pursued righteousness as if it came by works, and they stumbled over the stumbling stone. He places the stone image beside the promise that the one who believes will not be put to shame.

John's warning to the Pharisees and Sadducees who came to his baptism: produce fruit in keeping with repentance, and do not rely on Abraham, for the axe is at the root of the trees. The call for fruit in 21:43 repeats the Baptist's demand, and it is no accident that the passage opens with a question about John.

God spoke through the prophets in many ways, but in these last days He has spoken by His Son, whom He appointed heir of all things. The line is almost a commentary on the parable, with its servants and then a Son, and the Son as heir.

Paul's olive tree guards against a hard reading of Matthew 21:43. Branches have been broken off because of unbelief and wild shoots grafted in, but God is able to graft the natural branches in again. The tenants are replaced, yet the root remains the same.

study.oneStory:
God made the world as a place to share with His image-bearers, and He gave them a garden to work and keep, Genesis 2:15. From the first the human calling was stewardship: a gift received, a task given, and an account to be rendered. When the first couple took what was not theirs, the story of entrusting and failing began. The tenants of Matthew 21 are the latest in a line that runs from Eden through Israel's kings and priests, and the parable is the clearest statement of the pattern in the Gospels.

Israel was God's vine, and in the Law and the Prophets the LORD looked for fruit, justice, mercy and faithfulness. The prophets were His servants, sent to call the nation back, and the record is that they were mistreated. Here Jesus draws the whole history into a single scene and adds the unexpected twist: after the servants, the Son. The story that began with a garden given to a man is now at the point where the owner's own heir stands in the vineyard.

The passage also answers a question the Gospels keep raising: how can the Messiah be rejected by those who know the Scriptures? The answer is that Scripture foretold it. The psalm says the builders reject the stone and the Lord reverses it. The cross is not an interruption of the plan but its centre. Peter and Paul will preach it that way, and the church will be built on that stone.

The kingdom, then, is not removed from the world but given to a people who bear fruit. In Acts it is given to Jews and then Gentiles, and the vineyard is enlarged. The new people are called a chosen people, a royal priesthood and a holy nation, 1 Peter 2:9, and their fruit is the life of the Spirit, Galatians 5:22-23.

The story ends with the vineyard restored. Isaiah had promised a day when God would say of His vineyard, 'Sing about a fruitful vineyard,' and that Israel would 'fill the whole world with fruit,' Isaiah 27:2-6. In the new creation the river of life flows from the throne, and on either side is the tree of life with its fruit and leaves for the healing of the nations, Revelation 22:1-2. The tenants who failed are replaced by a people who bear fruit because they abide in the Son, and the stone the builders rejected is the foundation of a city whose builder and maker is God, Hebrews 11:10.

quiz.q: How did Jesus respond to the demand to know His authority?

options.text: He asked whether John's baptism was from heaven, exposing their refusal to reckon honestly with the truth.
options.note: Verses 24-27 show Jesus' counter-question unmasking their bad faith.

options.text: He refused to answer and said nothing further.
options.note: He did decline to answer directly, but only after exposing them with a probing question, which this omits.

options.text: He immediately claimed to be the Son of God.
options.note: He revealed His identity through parables here rather than a direct claim to them.

options.text: He admitted He had no authority to act.
options.note: His whole response assumes His authority is from heaven.

quiz.q: What does the parable of the two sons teach?

options.text: Real obedience, not mere words, does the Father's will, so repentant outcasts enter ahead of those who only profess.
options.note: Verses 28-32 contrast saying and doing, exalting repentance.

options.text: It is better to say yes to God even if you do not follow through.
options.note: The opposite; the son who said yes but did nothing failed to do the Father's will.

options.text: Both sons pleased the father equally in the end.
options.note: Only the first, who actually went, did the father's will.

options.text: God cares only about outward words of commitment.
options.note: The parable prizes doing over merely saying.

quiz.q: In the parable of the tenants, who is the son who is killed?

options.text: Jesus, the beloved Son sent last, rejected and killed, foretelling His own death.
options.note: The son sent after the servants pictures Jesus and His coming crucifixion.

options.text: One of the prophets sent to Israel.
options.note: The prophets are the earlier servants; the son is distinct and greater, pointing to Jesus.

options.text: John the Baptist, the last messenger before Jesus.
options.note: John is among the messengers, but the son is the owner's own heir, Jesus Himself.

options.text: A symbol with no particular fulfillment.
options.note: Jesus clearly intends the son to represent Himself, as the leaders perceive.

quiz.q: What does Jesus mean that the kingdom will be given to a people who produce its fruit?

options.text: It is taken from the fruitless stewards and given to the fruit-bearing people God gathers in Christ.
options.note: Verse 43 ties belonging to the kingdom to bearing fruit for God.

options.text: God will replace the leaders with better human rulers.
options.note: New leadership is involved, but the point is a fruit-bearing people, not merely swapping rulers.

options.text: The kingdom depends on producing enough religious works.
options.note: The fruit flows from genuine faith and repentance, not mere works to earn the kingdom.

options.text: God has abandoned the idea of a kingdom altogether.
options.note: The kingdom continues, given to those who bear its fruit.

questions: The leaders would not answer honestly about John because it cost them too much. Where are you avoiding a truth about Jesus because of what it would require?
One son said no but obeyed, the other said yes but did not. Which son are you more like right now, and where is the gap between your words and your obedience?
Tax collectors and prostitutes entered ahead of the respectable. How does that unsettle any confidence you place in your religious standing rather than in repentance?
The owner kept sending messengers and finally his Son. How have you responded to God's patient pursuit of you, and to the Son He sent?
The stone men rejected became the cornerstone. Is Jesus the foundation you are building on, or a stone you keep stumbling over?

translationNotes.note: Manuscripts vary in the order of the two sons and in which answer the leaders give; in every form the point is unchanged, that doing the father's will, not merely saying yes, is what counts.
The quotation is Psalm 118:22-23; the word rendered cornerstone is literally the head of the corner, the crucial stone of a building, applied to the rejected and risen Christ.
A few early manuscripts do not include verse 44, which parallels Luke 20:18; it is retained here as in the BSB and pictures the stone that both saves and judges.
